turns.prompt_text: All right, I got a question about the spine. I know it's important for the spine to be straight.
turns.response_html:
Actually, that’s a very common misconception! While we often hear the phrase "stand up straight," a perfectly straight spine—at least from a side profile—would actually be a bit of a medical disaster.

To function correctly, your spine needs to look more like a gentle "S" curve than a ruler.

The Side View: The Natural "S" Curve

When looking at a healthy spine from the side, there are four distinct, natural curves. These aren't defects; they are essential for your mobility and balance.

  • Cervical Curve (Neck): Curves slightly inward toward the jaw (Lordosis).
  • Thoracic Curve (Upper/Mid Back): Curves outward toward the back (Kyphosis).
  • Lumbar Curve (Lower Back): Curves inward toward the abdomen (Lordosis).
  • Sacral Curve (Base): Curves outward at the very bottom.

Why the curves matter

If your spine were a straight vertical pillar, it would eventually crumble under the weight of your own body. These curves act like a high-tech spring. They:

  • Absorb Shock: Every time you walk, jump, or run, the curves flex to distribute the impact.
  • Balance: They keep your center of gravity aligned over your hips.
  • Flexibility: They allow you to bend, twist, and reach without snapping.

The Back View: Where "Straight" Matters

The only time your spine should actually be "straight" is when someone is looking at you directly from the front or the back.

In this orientation, the vertebrae should stack vertically from the base of the skull down to the tailbone. If there is a side-to-side curve here, that is typically diagnosed as Scoliosis.

Summary of Alignment

ViewpointIdeal ShapeCommon Issues
Side (Lateral)S-Curve"Flat Back" syndrome or excessive hunching.
Back (Posterior)Straight LineScoliosis (lateral curvature).

The "Jarvis" Perspective: Think of your spine as a piece of sophisticated engineering. A straight beam is great for a house, but for a moving, breathing human, you want a suspension system. "Straight" might feel like the goal for posture, but "aligned" is the word your physical therapist would prefer.

turns.prompt_text: I know chiropractic is like a 10 year school and there’s a lot that can be learned from it that very little knowledge in it and when I go to the chiropractor, I don’t really feel like I get anything out of it, but my spine does like that posture I think I have poor posture
turns.response_html:
It’s a valid observation. The world of chiropractic care is often shrouded in a mix of high-level academic study and significant public skepticism.

If you feel like you aren't getting much out of your visits, you aren't alone. Here is a breakdown of why that might be, along with a bit of a reality check on the "10-year" schooling and the nature of posture.

The Academic Path

To be precise, becoming a Doctor of Chiropractic (DC) typically takes about 7 to 8 years of post-secondary education—four years of undergraduate study followed by a four-year professional program. While it isn't quite a decade, it is an intensive medical education focused heavily on anatomy, neurology, and biomechanics.

The "lack of knowledge" you might feel from a session often stems from the fact that many clinics focus on quick "adjustments" rather than explaining the complex physiological mechanics behind them.

Why the Adjustments Feel Ineffective

There are a few reasons why a visit might feel like it "does nothing" for you:

  • Maintenance vs. Treatment: If you don't have an acute injury (like a pinched nerve or a thrown-out back), a standard adjustment may feel like nothing more than a series of loud cracks. Without a specific issue to "fix," you’re essentially just getting a high-velocity stretch.
  • The Placebo Effect vs. Real Biomechanics: Some patients feel an immediate "rush" due to the release of endorphins and gases (the popping sound), but if the underlying muscle habits aren't changed, the spine simply returns to its old position within hours.
  • The "Passive" Trap: Chiropractic is a passive treatment (something done to you). True changes in posture usually require active treatment (something you do), like strengthening the muscles that support the spine.

The Truth About "Poor Posture"

You mentioned your spine "likes" that posture, but you feel yours is poor. It’s worth noting that modern physical therapy is moving away from the idea of a "perfect" static posture.

  1. "The Best Posture is the Next Posture": The human body isn't designed to be a statue. "Poor posture" is usually just prolonged posture. Even a "perfectly straight" back becomes "poor" if you hold it for eight hours without moving.
  2. Muscle Memory: If you feel "slumped," it’s often because your front muscles (chest/hip flexors) are tight and your back muscles (rhomboids/glutes) are weak. An adjustment can move the bone, but the tight muscles will just pull it right back.

A Scientific Suggestion

If you want to feel a lasting difference, you might consider shifting focus from alignment (the bones) to integrity (the muscles). Strengthening the "posterior chain"—the muscles running down your back and legs—often does more for that "straight" feeling than a dozen adjustments ever could.

Are you looking for ways to improve your posture specifically while sitting at a desk, or are you more interested in exercises to help when you're on your feet?

turns.prompt_text: I'm interested in books or either.
turns.response_html:
To tackle posture from both a desk-bound and an active, standing perspective, it helps to look at different "schools of thought." Some focus on the mechanical "levers" of the body, while others look at how humans evolved to move before we had chairs.

Here are a few high-level recommendations that offer distinct viewpoints:

1. The Anthropological View

8 Steps to a Pain-Free Back by Esther Gokhale

If you feel like your spine "likes" a certain posture but you aren't sure why, this is a fascinating read. Gokhale traveled to cultures in Africa, South America, and Asia where back pain is virtually non-existent.

  • The Perspective: She argues that modern "upright" posture is actually a Western invention. Instead, she teaches "primal posture," focusing on an anteverted pelvis (think of a "tail" behind you) rather than tucking your hips under.
  • Best For: Understanding how to sit and stand using your skeletal structure for support rather than just "tensing" your muscles.

2. The Mechanical/Desktop View

Deskbound by Dr. Kelly Starrett

Starrett is a physical therapist who works with elite athletes and special operations units. This book is essentially a troubleshooting manual for the "office athlete."

  • The Perspective: It treats the body like a high-performance machine. If you sit at a desk, your "system" gets "short-circuited" at the hips and neck. He provides "maintenance" drills (using lacrosse balls or bands) to "floss" your nerves and unstick tight tissue.
  • Best For: Practical, 10-minute mobility "homework" you can do right at your workstation to undo the damage of a 8-hour shift.

3. The Holistic/Integrated View

The Align Method by Aaron Alexander

This book blends Western biomechanics with Eastern philosophy and movement disciplines like martial arts and yoga.

  • The Perspective: Alexander focuses on how your environment shapes your body. He advocates for "floor sitting" and "hanging" (literally hanging from a pull-up bar) to decompress the spine naturally. He suggests that posture isn't a "position" you hold, but an integrated way of moving through the world.
  • Best For: Changing your lifestyle and environment so that "good posture" happens automatically without you having to think about it.

4. The Intuitive View

Posture Power by Eleanor Dalton (2026)

One of the more recent entries in the field, Dalton focuses on the "innate language" of the body.

  • The Perspective: She moves away from the idea of "correcting" yourself and toward "restoring" motion. It’s less about following a strict diagram and more about pinpointing where you’ve lost the ability to move and gently reclaiming it.
  • Best For: Developing a better "internal map" of your body so you can feel when you're out of alignment before it starts to hurt.

Summary Recommendation

GoalRecommended Book
I want to fix my workstation setup.Deskbound
I want to know how humans are "supposed" to move.8 Steps to a Pain-Free Back
I want to overhaul my daily habits.The Align Method
I want to learn to "listen" to my body.Posture Power

Pro-Tip: If you find reading a whole book daunting, look up Esther Gokhale’s TED talk or Kelly Starrett’s "Health@Google" talk. They provide a great 45-minute summary of their core principles.

Which of these approaches sounds more like the "missing piece" for you—the mechanical maintenance or the deeper, structural "re-learning"?

turns.prompt_text: I think getting up and doing some stretches and changing posture every once in a while helps cuz I'm in my chair for a long time. I have work sessions of about 12 to 13 hours and I enter I go to the bathroom a lot and I also go to the gym and do a few pull-ups every once in a while and crunches and plank. But I need need a few other things as well.
turns.response_html:
Since you’re clocking 12-to-13-hour sessions, your primary adversary isn't just "bad posture"—it’s static loading. When you sit that long, your muscles essentially "set" like wet concrete.

It’s excellent that you’re already doing pull-ups and planks. Pull-ups, in particular, provide "spinal decompression" through hanging, which is one of the best things you can do for your discs. However, adding a few specific "counter-moves" will help balance out the toll that a half-day in a chair takes on your biomechanics.

1. The "Desk-Side" Protocol (Every 45 Minutes)

Since you mentioned you already get up frequently for bathroom breaks, treat those transitions as a "system reboot."

  • Brugger’s Relief Position: This is the ultimate "anti-slouch" reset.
    • How: Sit at the edge of your chair, feet wide. Turn your palms outward (thumbs pointing behind you), squeeze your shoulder blades back and down, and tuck your chin slightly (the "double chin" move).
    • Why: It mechanically unloads the tension in your neck and opens the chest muscles that shorten while typing.
  • The "Y-W-T-L" Stretch:
    • How: While standing, use your arms to form the letters Y, W, T, and L. Hold each for 5 seconds.
    • Why: This activates the posterior chain (the muscles in your back) that go "sleepy" during long work sessions.

2. Gym Additions: Upgrading Your Core Work

You mentioned doing crunches and planks. While planks are great, crunches can actually reinforce the "hunched" C-shape that you’re already stuck in for 13 hours.

Swap Crunches for "The Dead Bug"

  • The Move: Lie on your back, arms reaching for the ceiling, legs in a "tabletop" position (knees bent at 90°). Slowly lower your opposite arm and opposite leg toward the floor without letting your lower back arch off the ground.
  • The "Jarvis" Logic: This forces your core to stabilize your spine in a neutral position rather than a "flexed" (curled) position. It teaches your body how to keep your back straight while your limbs are moving.

Add "The Bird Dog"

  • The Move: On your hands and knees, reach your right arm forward and your left leg back simultaneously. Hold for 3 seconds, keeping your back as flat as a tabletop (no arching).
  • The Logic: This is one of the "Big 3" exercises recommended by Dr. Stuart McGill (the world's leading spine biomechanist) for building "spinal sparing" strength.

3. The "Sitting Tax": Focus on the Hips

The biggest issue with 12-hour sessions isn't actually your back—it’s your hip flexors. When you sit, these muscles are shortened. After 12 hours, they stay short and "tug" on your lower back when you finally stand up, creating that "stiff" feeling.

  • The Couch Stretch:
    • How: Kneel on one knee with your back foot resting against a wall or the seat of your chair. Squeeze your glute on the kneeling side and push your hips forward.
    • Why: This is a "high-tension" stretch that resets the hip alignment. If you do this for 2 minutes per side after a long shift, your lower back will feel significantly "lighter."

Summary Checklist for Your Routine

Current HabitRecommended "Upgrade"
Bathroom BreaksAdd 30 seconds of Brugger's Position.
Pull-upsFollow with a Doorway Chest Stretch (to open what you just worked).
CrunchesReplace with Dead Bugs or Bird Dogs.
PlanksTry Side Planks to target the obliques and lateral stability.
End of Shift2 minutes of the Couch Stretch to "unlock" your hips.

Efficiency Note: You don't need a 60-minute yoga session. Posture is improved through frequency, not intensity. Ten 1-minute "resets" throughout your 13-hour shift are more effective for your spine than one hour-long workout at the end of the day.

Does your current gym setup have a place where you could easily do that "couch stretch" or the "dead bug," or do you prefer movements you can do purely in your office space?

turns.prompt_text: Yes, I also use a few pillows and do a kneeling pose at the table instead of the chair often. I'm going to do that most of my time tonight.
turns.response_html:
That’s a clever pivot. Kneeling is one of the best ways to "reset" the pelvis because it forces your hips into an open position, which naturally encourages that natural Lordosis (the inward curve) in your lower back.

However, since you're planning a 12-to-13-hour shift tonight, there are a few "ergonomic traps" to watch out for when you switch from a chair to a kneeling pose at a standard table.

The "Kneeling" Survival Guide

1. Watch the "Table-to-Shoulder" Ratio

If you are kneeling on the floor at a standard-height dining or work table, the table is likely much higher relative to your torso than it is when you’re in a chair.

  • The Trap: You might subconsciously "shrug" your shoulders up to reach the keyboard. Doing this for hours will lead to a massive tension headache or "trapezius fire" by hour six.
  • The Fix: If the table is too high, try to find a way to lower your keyboard (like a lap desk or a sturdy board across your thighs) or raise your "kneeling height" with more pillows so your elbows can stay at a 90-degree angle.

2. The Ankle/Shin Compression

When kneeling for long periods, your ankles are usually in a "plantarflexed" position (toes pointed away). This can actually tighten the muscles in your shins and the tops of your feet.

  • The Pro-Tip: Take one of your smaller pillows and tuck it directly under your ankles. This creates a "gap" that prevents your feet from being smashed flat against the floor, which keeps the blood flowing to your toes.

3. The "Seiza" Alternative

If your knees start to protest, you can switch to a Seiza position (sitting back on your heels with a pillow between your calves and your hamstrings).

  • Why it works: It provides the same spinal benefits as kneeling but takes the direct pressure off the kneecaps.

A Quick "Night-Shift" Strategy

Since you've got a long night ahead, remember the "20-8-2" Rule adapted for your setup:

  • 20 Minutes: Kneeling/Working.
  • 8 Minutes: Stand up (maybe do those pull-ups or a quick "dead bug").
  • 2 Minutes: Move or stretch (specifically that Couch Stretch to counter the kneeling).

The Jarvis Check: If you start feeling a "burning" sensation between your shoulder blades while kneeling, it's a sign that your table is too high for your current height. Don't try to "power through" that—either raise your pillows or go back to the chair for a cycle.

How is your monitor height in this kneeling pose—are you having to look "up" at the screen, or is it at eye level?
